docs.title: qccodec
docs.text:
qccodec knows how to talk to quantum chemistry programs. For each program it has one codec that turns a qcdata ProgramInput into the program's native input files and command, and turns the program's output back into structured qcdata results.

qccodec never runs anything itself. qccompute runs the program and uses the codec on both ends, so most scientists use the two together.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install qccompute   # also installs qccodec

You also need the program itself; each program page says how to install it and get it found.

docs.title: Run a calculation
docs.text:
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure
from qccompute import compute

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="psi4",
    calctype=CalcType.gradient,
    structure=Structure(
        symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
        geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    ),
    model=Model(method="wb97x-d", basis="def2-svp"),
    keywords={"d_convergence": 1e-8},  # Psi4's own option names
)
output = compute(prog_input)
print(output.results.energy, output.results.gradient)

Every program page has complete, runnable scripts like this one for each calculation type it supports, with every common option shown and the program's quirks explained. Copy one, delete what you don't need, and run it.

    program: str,
    calctype: CalcType | str,
    *,
    stdout: str | None = None,
    directory: Any = None,
    input_data: ProgramInput | None = None,
    failed: bool = False,

    """Decode saved program output into structured data without running anything.

    Args:
        program: Name of the program that produced the output.
        calctype: The type of calculation that was run.
        stdout: The program's captured output.
        directory: The calculation directory holding output files.
        input_data: The input used for the calculation, for parsers that need it.
        failed: Recover available data from a failed calculation.
        options: Overrides for the codec's declared decode options.
        version: The program version, when the output does not print it.

    Returns:
        The qcdata model matching ``calctype``.

        calctype,
        stdout=stdout,
        directory=directory,
        input_data=input_data,
        failed=failed,

def get_codec(program: str | Inputs) -> Codec:
    """Resolve the codec for a program name or input object.

    Resolution order: codecs passed to ``register``, built-ins, then codecs installed
    by other packages under the ``qccodec.codecs`` entry point group. A ``FileInput``
    resolves to the pass-through file codec.

    Args:
        program: A program name, or an input whose program should be resolved.

    Raises:
        CodecNotFoundError: No codec is available for the program.
    """
    if isinstance(program, ProgramInput):
        name = program.program
    elif isinstance(program, FileInput):
        from .programs.file import codec as file_codec

        return file_codec
    else:
        name = program

    codec = _REGISTERED.get(name)
    if codec is None and name in _BUILTIN:
        module = import_module(f"qccodec.programs.{_BUILTIN[name]}")
        codec = module.codecs[name] if hasattr(module, "codecs") else module.codec
    if codec is None:
        codec = _plugin(name)
    if codec is None:
        raise CodecNotFoundError(f"No codec found for program '{name}'.")
    return codec

def register(codec: Codec) -> Codec:
    """Make a codec resolvable by its program name for this process.

    A registered codec takes precedence over a built-in with the same name, so
    scripts can both add new programs and override shipped integrations. The
    codec is returned so this can be used as a decorator-style one-liner.
    """
    _REGISTERED[codec.program] = codec
    return codec

docs.text:
Program-specific translation between qcdata objects and native inputs/outputs.

A codec encodes a ProgramInput into a SubprocessInput or PythonInput and decodes the native output back into a qcdata *Data object. File-based programs register small parsers with @codec.parser(...); Python-native programs supply a decode function instead.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default program str

Name matched against ProgramInput.program.

required calctypes Collection[CalcType | str]

Calculation types this codec can encode.

required options Mapping[str, Any] | None

Decode options and their defaults, e.g. what to collect. Values passed to decode/parse are validated against these keys and reach parsers as Context.options.

None encode Encoder | None

Translate an input into a native invocation. See encoder.

None decode Decoder | None

Translate native output into data. See decoder.

None failure Failure | None

Detect a failure the program reported. See failure.

None propagate_wfn PropagateWfn | None

(output, input_data) -> ProgramInput placing the wavefunction from a previous output onto the next input as a guess.

None version_key VersionKey | None

Turns the program's version string into a PEP 440 version for matching parser versions. Not needed when the program already prints versions like 6.1.0.

None parsers Iterable[ParserSpec]

Pre-built parser specifications.

def __init__(
    self,
    program: str,
    calctypes: Collection[CalcType | str],
    *,
    options: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    encode: Encoder | None = None,
    decode: Decoder | None = None,
    failure: Failure | None = None,
    propagate_wfn: PropagateWfn | None = None,
    version_key: VersionKey | None = None,
    parsers: Iterable[ParserSpec] = (),
) -> None:
    """Create a codec; hooks may also be attached later with decorators."""
    self.program: str = program
    self.calctypes: frozenset[CalcType] = frozenset(CalcType(c) for c in calctypes)
    self.options: dict[str, Any] = dict(options or {})
    self.propagate_wfn: PropagateWfn | None = propagate_wfn
    self.version_key: VersionKey | None = version_key
    self.parsers: list[ParserSpec] = list(parsers)
    self._encode: Encoder | None = encode
    self._decode: Decoder | None = None
    self._failure: Failure | None = failure
    if decode is not None:
        self.decoder(decode)

def decoder(self, func: F) -> F:
    """Register ``func(input_data, native_output) -> Data`` in place of parsers.

    Raises:
        RegistryError: The codec has parsers or options, which only the parser
            pipeline uses.
    """
    if self.parsers:
        raise RegistryError(
            f"Codec {self.program!r} has parsers; a decoder would replace them."
        )
    if self.options:
        raise RegistryError(
            f"Codec {self.program!r} declares options, which only parsers receive."
        )
    self._decode = func
    return func

def failure(self, func: F) -> F:
    """Register ``func(ctx) -> str | None`` returning a message if the program failed.

    A message makes decoding recover partial data and then raise
    ``CalculationError`` with that data attached.
    """
    self._failure = func
    return func

def parser(
    self,
    *,
    target: Target | None = None,
    calctypes: Collection[CalcType | str] | None = None,
    file: FileRef = STDOUT,
    required: bool = True,
    versions: str | None = None,
) -> Callable[[F], F]:
    """Register a parser function.

    Args:
        target: Result field to fill, or a tuple for a nested field. Directory
            parsers may omit it and return a mapping merged into the result.
        calctypes: Calculation types this parser applies to; all when omitted.
        file: ``"stdout"`` (default), ``"directory"`` (the parser receives a
            ``Context``), a file name/glob relative to the directory, or a
            function of the ``Context`` returning such a name.
        required: If True, a missing file or ``MatchNotFoundError`` fails
            decoding unless partial data is being recovered.
        versions: Program versions this parser applies to, as a PEP 440
            specifier such as ``">=6.0"`` or ``">=5.0,<6.0"``; every version
            when omitted. Parsers for the same target may coexist when each
            declares ``versions``.

    Returns:
        The original function, unchanged, so it can be called and tested directly.
    """
    types = (
        frozenset(CalcType)
        if calctypes is None
        else frozenset(CalcType(c) for c in calctypes)
    )
    try:
        specifier = SpecifierSet(versions) if versions is not None else None
    except InvalidSpecifier as exc:
        raise RegistryError(f"Invalid versions specifier {versions!r}.") from exc

    def decorate(func: F) -> F:
        """Validate and record the parser specification."""
        if self._decode is not None:
            raise RegistryError(
                f"Codec {self.program!r} has a decoder; parsers would never run."
            )
        if target is None and file != DIRECTORY:
            raise RegistryError(
                f"Parser '{func.__name__}' must have a target unless file='directory'."
            )
        if target is not None and not (
            isinstance(target, str)
            or (
                isinstance(target, tuple)
                and all(isinstance(k, str) for k in target)
            )
        ):
            raise RegistryError(
                f"Target {target!r} must be a string or tuple of strings."
            )
        if specifier is not None and target == VERSION_TARGET:
            raise RegistryError(
                "The program version parser runs on every version; "
                "it cannot declare versions."
            )
        for existing in self.parsers:
            if (
                target is not None
                and existing.target == target
                and types & existing.calctypes
                and (specifier is None or existing.versions is None)
            ):
                raise RegistryError(
                    f"Duplicate parser target {target!r} for overlapping "
                    "calculation types. Declare versions on both parsers if "
                    "they handle different program versions."
                )
        self.parsers.append(
            ParserSpec(func, file, types, required, target, specifier)
        )
        return func

    return decorate

def encode(self, input_data: Inputs) -> NativeInput:
    """Translate an input into a native invocation without executing it.

    Raises:
        EncoderError: The codec has no encoder, the input's program or
            calculation type is not supported, or the encoder returned
            something other than a ``SubprocessInput`` or ``PythonInput``.
    """
    if self._encode is None:
        raise EncoderError(f"Codec {self.program!r} has no encoder.")
    if isinstance(input_data, ProgramInput):
        if input_data.program != self.program:
            raise EncoderError(
                f"Codec {self.program!r} cannot encode {input_data.program!r}."
            )
        if input_data.calctype not in self.calctypes:
            raise EncoderError(
                f"{self.program} does not support {input_data.calctype.value}."
            )
    native = self._encode(input_data)
    if not isinstance(native, (SubprocessInput, PythonInput)):
        raise EncoderError(
            f"{self.program} encoder must return SubprocessInput or PythonInput, "
            f"not {type(native).__name__}."
        )
    return native

def decode(
    self,
    input_data: Inputs,
    native_output: NativeOutput,
    options: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Data:
    """Interpret native output, returning data or raising with partial data.

    When the run failed (for example a nonzero exit status), whatever can be
    parsed is recovered, and if the codec's failure hook explains the failure
    ``CalculationError`` carries that explanation and the recovered data.

    Args:
        input_data: The input that produced the output.
        native_output: What the runner observed.
        options: Overrides for this codec's declared ``options``.

    Raises:
        CalculationError: The program failed and the failure hook says why.
        ParserError: A required output is missing or malformed in a run that
            did not fail.
    """
    if self._decode is not None:
        self._merge_options(options)  # rejects unknown keys
        return self._decode(input_data, native_output)
    if not isinstance(input_data, ProgramInput):
        raise ParserError(f"Codec {self.program!r} has no decoder for file inputs.")
    return self.parse(
        input_data.calctype,
        stdout=native_output.stdout,
        directory=native_output.directory,
        input_data=input_data,
        failed=native_output.failed,
        options=options,
        report_failure=True,
    )

def parse(
    self,
    calctype: CalcType | str,
    *,
    stdout: str | None = None,
    directory: str | Path | None = None,
    input_data: ProgramInput | None = None,
    failed: bool = False,
    options: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    version: str | None = None,
    as_dict: bool = False,
    check_failure: bool = True,
    report_failure: bool | None = None,
) -> StructuredData | dict[str, Any]:
    """Run this codec's parsers over saved artifacts without running the program.

    Args:
        calctype: The type of calculation that produced the artifacts.
        stdout: The program's captured output.
        directory: The calculation directory holding output files.
        input_data: The input used for the calculation, for parsers that need it.
        failed: Recover what is available from a failed calculation. Missing
            files and values are tolerated; malformed values still fail.
        options: Overrides for this codec's declared ``options``.
        version: The program version, when the output does not print it or
            should be overridden. Otherwise the version parser supplies it.
        as_dict: Return the collected values instead of a validated model.
        check_failure: Run the codec's failure hook first. Nested decodes of
            partial logs turn this off.
        report_failure: Raise ``CalculationError`` when the failure hook
            explains a failure. Defaults to ``not failed``, so recovery mode
            returns partial data quietly; ``decode`` passes True so a program
            that exited with an error still reports why.

    Returns:
        The qcdata model for ``calctype``, or a dictionary when ``as_dict``.

    Raises:
        ParserError: A required file is missing or a value is malformed.
        MatchNotFoundError: A required parser found no match.
        CalculationError: The failure hook explained a failure and
            ``report_failure`` is true. Recovered data is attached to every
            exception as ``.data``.
    """
    ctx = Context(
        codec=self,
        calctype=CalcType(calctype),
        stdout=stdout,
        directory=Path(directory) if directory is not None else None,
        input_data=input_data,
        failed=failed,
        options=self._merge_options(options),
    )
    data_type = get_data_type(ctx.calctype)
    message = (
        self._failure(ctx) if self._failure is not None and check_failure else None
    )
    if message:
        ctx.failed = True
    collected: dict[str, Any] = {"provenance": {"program": self.program}}
    not_found: MatchNotFoundError | None = None
    missing: list[str] = []
    # With an unknown version, version-gated alternatives for one target are
    # tried in order; a miss only counts if no alternative fills the target.
    deferred: dict[object, MatchNotFoundError | str] = {}
    filled: set[object] = set()

    def partial() -> StructuredData:
        """Validate whatever has been collected so far."""
        return data_type(**collected)

    specs = [s for s in self.parsers if ctx.calctype in s.calctypes]
    if version is not None:
        ctx.version = version
        _assign(collected, VERSION_TARGET, version)
        specs = [s for s in specs if s.target != VERSION_TARGET]
    else:
        # The version parser runs first so later parsers can be filtered by it.
        specs.sort(key=lambda s: s.target != VERSION_TARGET)
    for spec in specs:
        name = spec.parser.__name__
        key: object = spec.target if spec.target is not None else name
        gated = spec.versions is not None
        matched = self._version_matches(spec, ctx.version)
        if matched is False:
            continue
        if matched is None and key in filled:
            continue  # an earlier alternative already handled this target
        try:
            value: Any = spec.parser(ctx.contents(spec))
        except FileNotFoundError as exc:
            logger.info("Parser %r: missing %s", name, exc.filename or exc)
            if spec.required and not ctx.failed:
                if matched is None and gated:
                    deferred.setdefault(key, str(exc.filename or exc))
                else:
                    missing.append(str(exc.filename or exc))
            continue
        except MatchNotFoundError as exc:
            logger.info("Parser %r found no match", name)
            if spec.required and not ctx.failed:
                if matched is None and gated:
                    deferred.setdefault(key, exc)
                elif not_found is None:
                    not_found = exc
            continue
        except ParserError as exc:
            exc.data = partial()
            raise
        if spec.target is None:
            for item_key, item in value.items():
                _assign(collected, item_key, item)
        else:
            _assign(collected, spec.target, value)
        if spec.target == VERSION_TARGET:
            ctx.version = value
        filled.add(key)
        deferred.pop(key, None)
        logger.debug("Parser %r filled %r", name, spec.target)

    for problem in deferred.values():
        if isinstance(problem, MatchNotFoundError):
            not_found = not_found or problem
        else:
            missing.append(problem)

    if not_found is not None:
        not_found.data = partial()
        raise not_found
    if missing:
        raise ParserError(
            "Missing required output artifact(s): "
            + ", ".join(sorted(set(missing))),
            data=partial(),
        )

def path(self, pattern: str) -> Path:
    """Resolve a file name or glob pattern to exactly one path in the directory.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: No directory is available or nothing matches.
        ParserError: The pattern matches more than one file.
    """
    if self.directory is None:
        raise FileNotFoundError(pattern)
    matches = sorted(p for p in self.directory.glob(pattern) if p.is_file())
    if not matches:
        raise FileNotFoundError(pattern)
    if len(matches) > 1:
        names = ", ".join(str(p.relative_to(self.directory)) for p in matches)
        raise ParserError(f"Pattern {pattern!r} matched several files: {names}")
    return matches[0]

docs.title: Testing codecs
docs.text:
Test helpers for codecs: fixture cases, a case runner, and a codec contract check.

A case is a directory holding one program run and what a codec must make of it::

tests/data/<program>/<case>/
    input.json      ProgramInput used for the run (program, calctype, structure, ...)
    expected.json   the qcdata *Data object the codec must produce
    stdout          captured program output (optional)
    <files>         output files at their real relative paths, e.g. scr.geom/optim.xyz
    case.json       optional settings: {"options": {...}, "failed": true,
                    "raises": "MatchNotFoundError", "directory": true}
    encoded/        optional: command.txt (one argument per line) and the native
                    input files codec.encode(input) must generate

cases(root) discovers every such directory below root; run_case checks encoding, the full decode, and each registered parser on its own file against the matching slice of expected.json; check_codec verifies the structural contract every codec must satisfy, with or without fixtures.

Typical test module::

import pytest
from qccodec import get_codec
from qccodec.testing import cases, run_case

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", cases("tests/data"), ids=str)
def test_case(case):
    run_case(get_codec(case.input_data.program), case)

def check_encoding(codec: Codec, case: Case, *, rtol: float = 1e-9) -> None:
    """Compare ``codec.encode(case.input_data)`` against the case's ``encoded/`` files."""
    assert case.encoded is not None, f"{case}: no encoded/ directory"
    native = codec.encode(case.input_data)
    command_file = case.encoded / "command.txt"
    if command_file.exists():
        assert isinstance(native, SubprocessInput), f"{case}: expected a subprocess"
        expected_command = command_file.read_text().splitlines()
        assert list(native.command) == expected_command, (
            f"{case}: command {list(native.command)!r} != {expected_command!r}"
        )
    for path in sorted(p for p in case.encoded.rglob("*") if p.is_file()):
        name = path.relative_to(case.encoded).as_posix()
        if name == "command.txt":
            continue
        assert name in native.files, f"{case}: encode() did not generate {name!r}"
        produced = native.files[name]
        expected_bytes = path.read_bytes()
        if isinstance(produced, bytes):
            assert produced == expected_bytes, f"{case}: {name} differs"
        else:
            expected_text = expected_bytes.decode()
            assert _unversioned(produced) == _unversioned(expected_text), (
                f"{case}: {name} differs:\n--- expected\n{expected_text}"
                f"--- produced\n{produced}"
            )

def check_parsers(
    codec: Codec, case: Case, *, rtol: float = 1e-9, atol: float = 0.0
) -> None:
    """Call every applicable parser directly and compare with its expected slice."""
    assert case.expected is not None
    expected = _normalize(case.expected)
    ctx = Context(
        codec=codec,
        calctype=case.input_data.calctype,
        stdout=case.stdout,
        directory=case.directory,
        input_data=case.input_data,
        failed=case.failed,
        options={**codec.options, **case.options},
    )
    for spec in codec.parsers:
        if ctx.calctype not in spec.calctypes:
            continue
        try:
            contents = ctx.contents(spec)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            continue
        where = f"{case} parser {spec.parser.__name__}"
        try:
            value = spec.parser(contents)
        except MatchNotFoundError:
            assert not spec.required or case.failed, (
                f"{where}: required parser found no match"
            )
            if spec.target is not None:
                found = _expected_slice(expected, spec.target)
                assert found in (None, [], {}), (
                    f"{where}: no match, but expected.json holds {found!r}"
                )
            continue
        if spec.target is None:
            for key, item in value.items():
                assert_data_equal(
                    item,
                    expected.get(key),
                    rtol=rtol,
                    atol=atol,
                    where=f"{where}.{key}",
                )
        else:
            assert_data_equal(
                value,
                _expected_slice(expected, spec.target),
                rtol=rtol,
                atol=atol,
                where=where,
            )

def run_case(
    codec: Codec, case: Case, *, rtol: float = 1e-9, atol: float = 0.0
) -> None:
    """Check a codec against one fixture case.

    Verifies, in order: the encoded native inputs when ``encoded/`` exists; the full
    decode, which must produce ``expected.json`` or raise the exception named in
    ``case.json`` with ``expected.json`` attached as partial data; and each registered
    parser applied directly to its own file.

    Raises:
        AssertionError: With a description of the first mismatch.
    """
    if case.encoded is not None:
        check_encoding(codec, case, rtol=rtol)
    kwargs: dict[str, Any] = dict(
        stdout=case.stdout,
        directory=case.directory,
        input_data=case.input_data,
        failed=case.failed,
        options=case.options or None,
    )
    if case.raises:
        exc_type = _exception_class(case.raises)
        try:
            codec.parse(case.input_data.calctype, **kwargs)
        except exc_type as exc:
            if case.expected is not None:
                assert_data_equal(
                    getattr(exc, "data", None),
                    case.expected,
                    rtol=rtol,
                    atol=atol,
                    where=f"{case} partial",
                )
        else:
            raise AssertionError(f"{case}: expected {case.raises} but decode succeeded")
        return
    assert case.expected is not None, (
        f"{case}: expected.json is required unless raises is set"
    )
    data = codec.parse(case.input_data.calctype, **kwargs)
    assert_data_equal(data, case.expected, rtol=rtol, atol=atol, where=str(case))
    if codec.parsers:
        check_parsers(codec, case, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)

def check_codec(
    codec: Codec,
    *,
    inputs: Iterable[ProgramInput] = (),
    calctypes: Collection[CalcType] | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Verify the structural contract every codec must satisfy.

    Checks that parser targets name real result fields for every calculation type
    they apply to, that decoding nothing in recovery mode yields a typed empty result
    and in strict mode raises with typed partial data, that option defaults are
    well formed, and that encoding each of ``inputs`` yields a native invocation whose
    files stay inside the calculation directory.

    Args:
        codec: The codec to check.
        inputs: Inputs the codec must be able to encode.
        calctypes: Calculation types to exercise; defaults to ``codec.calctypes``.

    Raises:
        AssertionError: Listing every problem found.
    """
    problems: list[str] = []
    types = list(calctypes if calctypes is not None else codec.calctypes)
    if not codec.program:
        problems.append("program name is empty")
    if not codec.calctypes:
        problems.append("no calctypes declared")
    for key in codec.options:
        if not isinstance(key, str) or not key:
            problems.append(f"option name {key!r} is not a non-empty string")

    for spec in codec.parsers:
        problems.extend(_check_spec(spec, types))

    if codec.parsers:
        for calctype in types:
            data_type = get_data_type(calctype)
            try:
                empty = codec.parse(calctype, failed=True)
            except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                problems.append(f"{calctype.value}: parse(failed=True) raised {exc!r}")
            else:
                if not isinstance(empty, data_type):
                    problems.append(
                        f"{calctype.value}: parse(failed=True) returned {type(empty).__name__}"
                    )
            try:
                codec.parse(calctype)
            except ParserError as exc:
                if not isinstance(exc.data, data_type):
                    problems.append(
                        f"{calctype.value}: strict parse raised without typed partial data"
                    )
            except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                problems.append(f"{calctype.value}: strict parse raised {exc!r}")

    for inp in inputs:
        try:
            native = codec.encode(inp)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
            problems.append(f"encode({inp.calctype.value}) raised {exc!r}")
            continue
        for name in native.files:
            if Path(name).is_absolute() or ".." in Path(name).parts:
                problems.append(
                    f"encode({inp.calctype.value}) file escapes directory: {name!r}"
                )
        if isinstance(native, SubprocessInput) and not native.command:
            problems.append(f"encode({inp.calctype.value}) returned an empty command")
        if isinstance(native, PythonInput) and not callable(native.function):
            problems.append(f"encode({inp.calctype.value}) function is not callable")

    gated = [
        spec.parser.__name__ for spec in codec.parsers if spec.versions is not None
    ]
    has_version_parser = any(spec.target == VERSION_TARGET for spec in codec.parsers)
    if gated and not has_version_parser:
        problems.append(
            f"parsers {gated} declare versions but no parser fills "
            f"{VERSION_TARGET!r}, so the version is only known when passed in"
        )

    if codec.propagate_wfn is not None and not callable(codec.propagate_wfn):
        problems.append("propagate_wfn is not callable")
    if problems:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"Codec {codec.program!r} failed checks:\n  " + "\n  ".join(problems)
        )

data.save("data.json")

from qcdata import SinglePointData
data = SinglePointData.open("data.json")

Many values live in output files rather than stdout. Pass the calculation directory, and the ProgramInput that produced the run when the codec needs it (optimization trajectories, for example):

from qcdata import ProgramInput

data = decode(
    "terachem",
    CalcType.optimization,
    stdout=Path("tc.out").read_text(),
    directory=Path("."),                         # holds scr.geometry/optim.xyz
    input_data=ProgramInput.open("input.json"),
)

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
qccodec terachem hessian tc.out > data.json          # stdout only
qccodec terachem optimization tc.out . > data.json   # stdout plus a directory

docs.title: Failed calculations
docs.text:
A failed run usually still has useful values in it. Decode it in recovery mode to get whatever can be parsed:

partial = decode("terachem", "gradient", stdout=logs, directory=scratch_dir, failed=True)

With failed=True, missing files and values are tolerated and the recovered data is returned. Without it, a missing required value raises ParserError (or MatchNotFoundError), and a program that reported failure raises CalculationError; either way the recovered data is attached as .data. Pass report_failure=True with failed=True to get the program's explanation as CalculationError as well. The CLI supports recovery with --failed.

docs.title: Encoding without running
docs.text:
encode produces the native input without running anything, which is useful for checking what a program will receive or running it yourself:

from qcdata import ProgramInput, Structure
from qccodec import encode

native = encode(
    ProgramInput(
        program="terachem",
        calctype="energy",
        structure=Structure.open("molecule.xyz"),
        model={"method": "wb97xd3", "basis": "def2-svp"},
    )
)
native.command  # ("terachem", "tc.in")
native.files    # {"tc.in": "...", "geometry.xyz": "..."}

encode returns a SubprocessInput (a command plus the files it needs) or a PythonInput (a callable plus its arguments).

docs.title: Writing a codec
docs.text:
Everything qccodec knows about a program lives in one Codec object: its name, the calculation types it supports, an encoder, and either a set of small parsers (file-based programs) or a decode function (Python APIs). Built-ins live in qccodec/programs/<name>.py, one file per program, and you can build your own in a script the same way:

from qcdata import CalcType, ProgramInput
from qccodec import Codec, SubprocessInput, re_search

codec = Codec("myprog", calctypes={CalcType.energy})

@codec.encoder
def encode(inp: ProgramInput) -> SubprocessInput:
    return SubprocessInput(
        command=("myprog", "run.inp"),
        files={"run.inp": f"{inp.model.method}\n{inp.structure.to_xyz()}"},
    )

@codec.parser(target="energy", calctypes=[CalcType.energy])
def parse_energy(stdout: str) -> float:
    return float(re_search(r"Total energy:\s+(-?\d+\.\d+)", stdout).group(1))

Then run it with qccompute, either explicitly or by name after registering it:

import qccodec, qccompute

output = qccompute.compute(input_data, codec=codec)

qccodec.register(codec)              # now resolvable as program="myprog",
output = qccompute.compute(input_data)   # including as a geomeTRIC gradient child

register() also lets you override a built-in codec by name for the current process.

docs.title: Parsers
docs.text:
A parser is a plain function from file contents to a value. The decorator records where the value goes and when the parser runs, and returns the function unchanged so it stays easy to test directly.

@codec.parser(target="energy", calctypes=[CalcType.energy, CalcType.gradient])
def parse_energy(stdout: str) -> float: ...                      # reads stdout (default)

@codec.parser(file="crest.engrad", target="gradient", calctypes=[CalcType.gradient])
def parse_gradient(contents: str) -> list[list[float]]: ...      # reads a named file or glob

@codec.parser(file="directory", target="trajectory", calctypes=[CalcType.optimization])
def parse_trajectory(ctx: Context) -> list[ProgramOutput]: ...   # needs several files
  • target is the result field to fill, or a tuple for nested fields such as ("provenance", "program_version"). Directory parsers may omit it and return a mapping that is merged into the result.
  • calctypes restricts when the parser runs; omit it to run for every calculation type.
  • file is "stdout" (default), "directory", a file name or glob relative to the calculation directory, or a function of the Context returning such a name.
  • required=False tolerates a missing file or MatchNotFoundError.
  • versions=">=6.0" limits a parser to some program versions (a PEP 440 specifier); omit it to run on every version. See Program versions below.

Directory parsers receive a Context with stdout, directory, input_data, failed, options, path(pattern), read(pattern), and decode(calctype, stdout=...) for nested decoding with the same codec.

docs.title: Failure detection and Python-native programs
docs.text:
@codec.failure
def failure(ctx: Context) -> str | None:
    return "CREST reported FAILED." if "FAILED" in (ctx.stdout or "") else None

Many programs exit 0 after failing (TeraChem prints Job finished: only on success). When the hook returns a message, decoding recovers what it can and raises CalculationError with that data attached. This also happens when the program exits with an error, so the hook's explanation reaches the user rather than just an exit status. parse(..., failed=True) stays quiet and returns the recovered data; pass report_failure=True to raise the explanation there too. Programs driven through a Python API skip parsers entirely:

codec = Codec("mlp", calctypes={CalcType.energy, CalcType.gradient}, encode=encode, decode=decode)

where decode(input_data, native_output) maps native_output.value into a qcdata object.

docs.title: Options and wavefunction propagation
docs.text:
A codec declares the decode options it accepts, with defaults. Callers override them per calculation and parsers read them from the context:

codec = Codec("crest", calctypes={...}, options={"collect_rotamers": False})

@codec.parser(file="directory", calctypes=[CalcType.conformer_search])
def parse_rotamers(ctx: Context) -> dict:
    if not ctx.options["collect_rotamers"]:
        return {}
    ...

decode("crest", "conformer_search", directory=d, input_data=inp, options={"collect_rotamers": True})
qccompute.compute(inp, options={"collect_rotamers": True})

Unknown option names raise EncoderError. For optimizers that chain calculations, a codec may set codec.propagate_wfn = fn where fn(output, input_data) returns a new input carrying the previous output's wavefunction as the initial guess; TeraChem copies c0/ca0/cb0 and sets guess. qccompute calls it when propagate_wfn=True.

docs.title: Program versions
docs.text:
When a program changes its output format, register a parser per version range on the same target; the parser functions themselves stay version-free:

@codec.parser(target="gradient", calctypes=[CalcType.gradient], versions="<6.0")
def parse_gradient_v5(stdout: str) -> list[list[float]]: ...

@codec.parser(target="gradient", calctypes=[CalcType.gradient], versions=">=6.0")
def parse_gradient(stdout: str) -> list[list[float]]: ...

The parser targeting ("provenance", "program_version") runs first and its value selects which parsers apply. Programs whose version strings are not PEP 440 give the codec a version_key (TeraChem compares builds by release date, so v1.9-2023.08-dev matches versions=">=2023.8"). When no version can be read, alternatives for a target are tried in registration order and the first match wins. Pass version= to decode/parse for logs that never print one.

docs.title: Codecs from other packages
docs.text:
A package can ship a codec by publishing it as an entry point; get_codec and qccompute.compute then find it by program name with no registration call:

[project.entry-points."qccodec.codecs"]
myprog = "mypackage.codec:codec"

docs.title: Testing a codec
docs.text:
qccodec.testing gives every codec the same test harness. A recorded program run is a directory holding the inputs, the outputs, and the data the codec must produce:

tests/data/myprog/water_energy/
    input.json      ProgramInput used for the run
    expected.json   the qcdata *Data object the codec must produce
    stdout          captured program output
    <files>         output files at their real relative paths, e.g. scr.geom/optim.xyz
    case.json       optional: {"options": {...}, "failed": true, "raises": "ParserError"}
    encoded/        optional: command.txt plus the native input files encode() must write

import pytest
from qccodec import get_codec
from qccodec.testing import cases, check_codec, run_case

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", cases("tests/data"), ids=str)
def test_case(case):
    run_case(get_codec(case.input_data.program), case)

def test_contract():
    check_codec(codec, inputs=[some_program_input])

run_case checks the encoded files, the full decode (or the expected exception and its partial data), and every registered parser applied directly to its own file against the matching slice of expected.json. check_codec verifies the structural contract: parser targets name real result fields, decoding nothing yields typed empty data in recovery mode and typed partial data on error, and encoded files stay inside the directory.

CONTRIBUTING.md walks through adding a program to qccodec step by step, including the example scripts every program needs.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text: Each program page explains how qccodec maps a ProgramInput onto that program, then gives a complete example script for every calculation type it supports. The scripts run as written (they are tested), show every common option, and document the program's quirks for that kind of calculation.

docs.title: Conventions shared by every program
docs.text:
• Keywords are the program's own. ProgramInput.keywords pass through to the program in its native form, so the program's documentation applies. The program pages say where each codec puts them (an input file, command-line flags, a TOML document, ...).
  • Structured data stays structured. The method and basis go in model; the geometry, charge, and multiplicity go in structure. Codecs reject keywords that duplicate them.
  • Atom indices are 0-based, matching structure. Codecs convert them for programs that count from 1; files you supply verbatim (such as an xtb xcontrol) use the program's own convention.
  • Results describe your structure exactly. Codecs stop programs from moving, reorienting, or symmetrizing the molecule, so gradients, Hessians, and trajectories line up with the input.
  • Coordinates are in bohr and energies in Hartree, as everywhere in qcdata.
  • Errors carry the program's explanation. When a program fails, the error message says why, and any partial results are attached.

docs.title: Finding the program
docs.text: qccompute runs a program by name from PATH. To use a different build, or one that isn't on PATH, pass compute(..., executables={"orca": "/path/to/orca"}) or set QCCOMPUTE_ORCA_EXECUTABLE (the program name in capitals).

docs.title: xtb or CREST?
docs.text: Both run the GFN-xTB methods and give the same GFN2-xTB energies and gradients. Use program="xtb" for single points, Hessians, and optimizations with xtb's full set of options, and for g-xTB. Use program="crest" for conformer searches and CREST's other workflows.

docs.title: Optimizations: the program's optimizer or geomeTRIC?
docs.text: Programs with their own optimizer (CREST, ORCA, Psi4, TeraChem, xtb) run optimization themselves. geomeTRIC can drive any program's gradients instead, which is useful for a consistent optimizer across programs, constraints, and QM/MM optimizations with Psi4 point charges.

docs.title: CREST
docs.text:
CREST: write input.toml, run crest input.toml, and parse its output files.

Inputs map to CREST 3's TOML input as follows:

  • keywords are the TOML document itself, so CREST's own input-file keys apply: top-level settings such as threads or runtype, and sections such as {"calculation": {"level": [{"alpb": "water"}]}} or {"cregen": {...}}. CREST stops on keys it does not know.
  • model.method (gfn2, gfn1, gfn0, gfnff, ...) and the structure's charge and multiplicity are written into every [[calculation.level]]; setting charge or uhf in keywords is an error.
  • runtype defaults from the calculation type (singlepoint, numhess, optimize, imtd-gc); a given runtype must match it, e.g. nci or entropy for conformer searches.
  • threads defaults to the number of CPUs, at most 16. CREST itself always runs with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 and parallelizes over its own threads.

Calculation types: energy, gradient, hessian (numerical: also frequencies and normal modes), optimization, and conformer_search. Rotamers are parsed only with the decode option {"collect_rotamers": True}; there can be thousands. CREST optimizes with the center of mass at the origin; the codec shifts optimization trajectories back into the input's frame. No input field carries atom indices.

CREST computes GFN-xTB and GFN-FF with its built-in tblite and gfnff libraries, so it needs no separate xtb. Use the official static build: conda-forge's CREST 3.0.2 crashes in its optimizer.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Each script runs as written. Copy it, delete the options you don't need, and run it with python script.py. They live in the repository's examples/ folder.

docs.title: Single point: energy, gradient, Hessian
docs.text:
examples/crest/single_point.py

"""CREST single point: GFN-xTB or GFN-FF energy, gradient, or Hessian.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and CREST 3 on PATH, the
official static build from https://github.com/crest-lab/crest/releases (conda-forge's
CREST 3.0.2 crashes in its optimizer). CREST computes GFN-xTB and GFN-FF with its
built-in tblite and gfnff libraries, so no separate xtb is needed.

How the codec talks to CREST (https://crest-lab.github.io/crest-docs/page/documentation/inputfiles.html):

- ``keywords`` are CREST's TOML input file as a dictionary: top-level settings such
  as ``threads``, and sections such as ``calculation``. CREST stops on any key it
  does not know, so typos fail loudly.
- ``model.method`` ("gfn2", "gfn1", "gfn0", "gfnff") and the structure's charge and
  multiplicity are written into every ``[[calculation.level]]``; level settings
  (solvent, electronic temperature, accuracy) go in the one level shown below. Do
  not set ``charge`` or ``uhf`` in keywords.
- ``runtype`` comes from the calculation type ("singlepoint" or "numhess").
- The Hessian is numerical and comes with harmonic frequencies and normal modes.
- For xtb's full set of options (and g-xTB), use program "xtb" (examples/xtb/).
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy, CalcType.hessian

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,  # open shells: CREST gets multiplicity - 1 unpaired electrons
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="crest",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),  # or "gfn1", "gfn0", "gfnff"
    keywords={
        # Top-level CREST settings:
        "threads": 1,  # default: number of CPUs, at most 16
        # Settings for the method itself, one [[calculation.level]] table:
        "calculation": {
            "level": [
                {
                    "alpb": "water",  # implicit solvent; or "gbsa": "water"
                    # "etemp": 300.0,  # electronic temperature (K)
                    # "accuracy": 1.0,  # SCC accuracy; lower is tighter
                    # "maxscc": 300,  # maximum SCC iterations
                }
            ]
        },
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=600,  # seconds before CREST is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file in output.results.files
    # executables={"crest": "/path/to/crest"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_CREST_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
if results.hessian is not None:
    print("Frequencies (cm^-1):", results.freqs_wavenumber)
print("CREST version:", results.provenance.program_version)

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
examples/crest/optimization.py

"""CREST geometry optimization with its built-in ANCopt optimizer.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and CREST 3 on PATH, the
official static build from https://github.com/crest-lab/crest/releases (conda-forge's
CREST 3.0.2 crashes in its optimizer). No separate xtb is needed.

Notes for CREST optimizations (https://crest-lab.github.io/crest-docs/):

- Optimizer settings live in the ``calculation`` section of CREST's TOML input:
  ``optlev`` ("crude", "sloppy", "loose", "normal", "tight", "vtight", "extreme")
  and ``maxcycle``. Method settings (solvent, electronic temperature, ...) go in its
  ``level`` table, as in single_point.py. CREST stops on keys it does not know.
- Each step in ``results.trajectory`` has its structure and energy; the last step
  also has the gradient.
- For transition states, or an optimizer with more control, drive CREST gradients
  with geomeTRIC (examples/geometric/).
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="crest",
    calctype=CalcType.optimization,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),  # or "gfn1", "gfnff"
    keywords={
        "threads": 1,  # default: number of CPUs, at most 16
        "calculation": {
            # ANCopt settings:
            "optlev": "tight",  # convergence level
            "maxcycle": 100,  # maximum optimization steps
            # The method's settings:
            "level": [
                {
                    "alpb": "water",  # implicit solvent; or "gbsa": "water"
                    # "etemp": 300.0,  # electronic temperature (K)
                }
            ],
        },
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=600,  # seconds before CREST is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file (crestopt.xyz, ...) in results.files
    # executables={"crest": "/path/to/crest"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_CREST_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Energies (Hartree):", results.energies)
print("Final gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.trajectory[-1].results.gradient)
print("Final structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)
# Save the trajectory, e.g. to view in a molecule viewer:
# results.save("optimization.json"); results.final_structure.save("final.xyz")

docs.title: Conformer search
docs.text:
examples/crest/conformer_search.py

"""CREST conformer search (iMTD-GC: metadynamics, then optimization and sorting).

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and CREST 3 on PATH, the
official static build from https://github.com/crest-lab/crest/releases. No separate
xtb is needed.

Notes for CREST conformer searches (https://crest-lab.github.io/crest-docs/):

- The default workflow is iMTD-GC (``runtype = "imtd-gc"``). Other conformer
  workflows: "imtd-smtd", "entropy", "nci", "nci-mtd"; any other runtype is an error
  for this calculation type.
- Searches are long: minutes to hours for drug-sized molecules. GFN-FF ("gfnff") is
  much faster than GFN2-xTB and is a common choice for the search itself.
- ``model.method`` applies to every level of the calculation, so a GFN-FF search
  with GFN2-xTB re-ranking needs two runs: search here, then single points or
  optimizations of the conformers you keep.
- ``cregen`` settings control how structures are sorted and deduplicated: ``ewin``
  (energy window, kcal/mol), ``ethr`` (energy threshold, kcal/mol), ``rthr`` (RMSD
  threshold, angstrom), ``bthr`` (rotational-constant threshold).
- ``results.conformers`` are sorted by energy, lowest first; ``conformer_energies``
  are in Hartree. Rotamers (often thousands) are read only when asked for, with
  ``options={"collect_rotamers": True}``.
- Water has a single conformer; replace it with your molecule (Structure.open reads
  an xyz file in angstrom) and expect a longer run.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="crest",
    calctype=CalcType.conformer_search,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="gfnff"),  # or "gfn2" (slower)
    keywords={
        "threads": 4,  # default: number of CPUs, at most 16
        # "runtype": "nci",  # for non-covalent clusters; default "imtd-gc"
        # "topo": False,  # allow changes in bonding topology between conformers
        "calculation": {
            "level": [
                {
                    "alpb": "water",  # implicit solvent; or "gbsa": "water"
                }
            ],
        },
        # Sorting and deduplication of the ensemble:
        "cregen": {
            "ewin": 6.0,  # keep conformers within 6 kcal/mol of the lowest
            # "ethr": 0.05,  # energy threshold for duplicates (kcal/mol)
            # "rthr": 0.125,  # RMSD threshold for duplicates (angstrom)
            # "bthr": 0.01,  # rotational-constant threshold for duplicates
        },
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # options={"collect_rotamers": True},  # also read crest_rotamers.xyz
    # timeout=3600,  # seconds before CREST is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file in output.results.files
    # executables={"crest": "/path/to/crest"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_CREST_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Conformers:", len(results.conformers))
lowest = results.conformer_energies[0]
for i, energy in enumerate(results.conformer_energies):
    print(f"  {i}: {energy:.8f} Hartree, {(energy - lowest) * 627.5095:.2f} kcal/mol")
print("Lowest conformer (bohr):\n", results.conformers[0].geometry)
# Save the ensemble, e.g. one xyz file per conformer:
# for i, conformer in enumerate(results.conformers):
#     conformer.save(f"conformer_{i}.xyz")

docs.title: geomeTRIC
docs.text:
geomeTRIC: optimizations and transition-state searches driving another program.

geomeTRIC runs in Python and asks for gradients through a callback: every step is a full gradient calculation of the program named in subprograms, run by qccompute like any other calculation and kept in the trajectory. Any codec with gradients works as the child, including ones registered with qccodec.register.

Inputs map to geomeTRIC as follows:

  • subprograms must hold one ProgramSpec with calctype="gradient": the child program, its model, and its own keywords (passed to that program unchanged).
  • keywords are geomeTRIC's optimizer parameters (geometric.params.OptParams): maxiter, convergence_set, convergence_energy, trust, hessian, enforce, ... Two are handled by the codec: coordsys (tric by default, or cart, prim, dlc, hdlc) and constraints (geomeTRIC's constraint dictionary, e.g. {"freeze": [{"type": "xyz", "indices": [0]}]}, with set distances in bohr; scans are not supported).
  • cmdline_args are not accepted.

Calculation types: optimization and transition_state (transition=True; geomeTRIC computes a starting Hessian from finite differences of child gradients).

The trajectory holds one frame per optimizer step. Gradients at the displaced geometries of a finite-difference Hessian are not steps, so they are left out, unless one fails. Each Hessian geomeTRIC computes is attached to the frame at its geometry (frame.results.hessian): the first frame for hessian="first", the default for transition states, and also the last frame for "first+last" or "last". Atom indices in constraints are 0-based, as in geomeTRIC's Python interface.

With qccompute, propagate_wfn=True starts each child calculation from the previous step's orbitals when the child codec supports it (TeraChem).

docs.text: Each script runs as written. Copy it, delete the options you don't need, and run it with python script.py. They live in the repository's examples/ folder.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
examples/geometric/optimization.py

"""geomeTRIC geometry optimization driving another program's gradients.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute qccodec[geometric]`` (geomeTRIC itself) and the
gradient program on PATH. This example uses CREST for fast GFN2-xTB gradients:
https://github.com/crest-lab/crest/releases (official static build).

How it works (https://geometric.readthedocs.io/):

- geomeTRIC runs in Python and asks for a gradient at every step. Each one is a full
  ``gradient`` calculation of the program in ``subprograms``, with that program's own
  model and keywords, so any program with gradients works: CREST, xtb, Psi4, ORCA,
  TeraChem, ... Swap the ``ProgramSpec`` below for one of the commented alternatives.
- ``keywords`` are geomeTRIC's optimizer parameters (``geometric.params.OptParams``,
  the long ``geometric-optimize --help`` names). geomeTRIC ignores names it does not
  know, so check spelling against its documentation.
- ``coordsys``: "tric" (default, translation-rotation internal coordinates, good for
  several molecules), "dlc", "prim", or "cart".
- ``constraints`` use geomeTRIC's dictionary format with 0-based atom indices,
  distances in bohr, and angles in degrees. Scans are not supported.
- Every step in ``results.trajectory`` is the child's full output (energy, gradient,
  charges, ...), whichever program it is.
- QM/MM: this is the way to optimize a QM region in point charges with Psi4, since
  Psi4 1.11's own optimizer cannot (see the Psi4 child below). The charges stay fixed.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, ProgramSpec, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

# The program that computes energies and gradients: CREST with GFN2-xTB.
gradient_program = ProgramSpec(
    program="crest",
    calctype=CalcType.gradient,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),
    keywords={"threads": 1, "calculation": {"level": [{"alpb": "water"}]}},
)

# xtb instead (examples/xtb/single_point.py lists its keywords):
# gradient_program = ProgramSpec(
#     program="xtb",
#     calctype=CalcType.gradient,

"""geomeTRIC transition-state search driving another program's gradients.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute qccodec[geometric]`` (geomeTRIC itself) and the
gradient program on PATH. This example uses CREST for fast GFN2-xTB gradients:
https://github.com/crest-lab/crest/releases (official static build).

Notes for geomeTRIC transition-state searches (https://geometric.readthedocs.io/):

- ``CalcType.transition_state`` turns on geomeTRIC's saddle-point optimizer.
  geomeTRIC needs a starting Hessian, which it builds by finite differences of child
  gradients (two per Cartesian coordinate). Those displaced gradients are not
  optimizer steps, so ``results.trajectory`` leaves them out: it holds one frame per
  step, and each Hessian geomeTRIC computes is attached to the frame at its
  geometry (``frame.results.hessian``).
- ``"hessian"`` chooses when: ``"first"`` (the default) at the start,
  ``"first+last"`` also at the end, which is how this example checks its result,
  ``"each"`` at every step (costly).
- Start close to the saddle point. This example starts from nearly planar ammonia;
  its inversion transition state is planar, with one imaginary frequency.
- A transition state has exactly one negative Hessian eigenvalue (one imaginary
  frequency). The final frame's Hessian shows it, whatever the child program.
- The child program, coordinate systems, constraints, and QM/MM point charges work
  as in optimization.py; swap the ``ProgramSpec`` for xtb, Psi4, TeraChem, ...
- Transition-state steps use a small trust radius by default (``trust`` 0.01,
  ``tmax`` 0.03 angstrom), so expect more steps than for a minimum.
"""

import numpy as np
from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, ProgramSpec, Structure

# Ammonia near its planar inversion saddle point, coordinates in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["N", "H", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[
        [0.0, 0.0, 0.01],
        [1.88, 0.0, 0.01],
        [-0.94, 1.62, 0.01],
        [-0.94, -1.62, 0.01],
    ],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

# The program that computes energies and gradients: CREST with GFN2-xTB.
gradient_program = ProgramSpec(
    program="crest",
    calctype=CalcType.gradient,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),
    keywords={"threads": 1},  # add "calculation": {"level": [{"alpb": "water"}]}
)

# Psi4 instead (any gradient program works; see optimization.py for more):
# gradient_program = ProgramSpec(
#     program="psi4",
#     calctype=CalcType.gradient,
#     model=Model(method="wb97x-d", basis="def2-svp"),
#     cmdline_args=["-n", "1", "--memory", "2GB"],
# )

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="geometric",
    calctype=CalcType.transition_state,
    structure=structure,
    subprograms=[gradient_program],
    keywords={
        "coordsys": "tric",  # or "dlc", "prim", "cart"
        "maxiter": 100,
        "convergence_set": "gau",  # or "gau_tight", ...
        "hessian": "first+last",  # exact Hessians at the start and the end
        # "trust": 0.01,  # starting trust radius (angstrom)
        # "tmax": 0.03,  # largest trust radius (angstrom)
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # propagate_wfn=True,  # TeraChem: start each step from the previous orbitals
    # timeout=3600,
)

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Transition-state energy (Hartree):", results.energies[-1])
print("Transition-state structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)

# Confirm the saddle point: exactly one negative eigenvalue of the final Hessian.
final_hessian = results.trajectory[-1].results.hessian
eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(final_hessian)
print("Negative Hessian eigenvalues:", int((eigenvalues < -1e-3).sum()), "(1 for a TS)")

docs.title: ORCA
docs.text:
ORCA: write orca.inp, run orca orca.inp, and parse stdout and output files.

Inputs map to ORCA as follows:

  • model.method and model.basis start the simple-input line, ! method basis. Extra simple-input words, such as CPCM(water), TightSCF, or D3BJ, can go in model.method after the method name. Leave basis empty for composite methods.
  • The calculation type adds ! energy/engrad/freq/opt/optts. {"numgrad": True} and {"numfreq": True} request numerical derivatives.
  • A keyword set to True adds a simple-input word, so {"tightscf": True} writes ! tightscf; False or None leaves it out. Any other non-dictionary value is an error, so nothing is dropped silently.
  • {"maxcore": 2000} and {"pal": 4} become %maxcore and %pal nprocs.
  • A keyword whose value is a dictionary becomes an input block: {"scf": {"maxiter": 200}} writes %scf maxiter 200 end. Keys are kept as written; ORCA ignores case.
  • The structure is written to geometry.xyz with its charge and multiplicity. Setting coords, or method/basis inside a block, is an error.
  • cmdline_args are appended to the orca command.

Calculation types: energy, gradient, hessian (also the gradient when ORCA writes it), optimization, and transition_state (OptTS; give ORCA a starting Hessian, e.g. {"geom": {"calc_hess": True}}). ORCA keeps the input's coordinates and atom order. No input field carries atom indices.

Run ORCA by its full path: its parallel runs need it, and on many Linux desktops /usr/bin/orca is the GNOME screen reader. qccompute always runs the absolute path; put ORCA first on PATH or set QCCOMPUTE_ORCA_EXECUTABLE.

"""ORCA single point: energy, gradient, or Hessian.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and ORCA, free for academic
use from https://orcaforum.kofo.mpg.de. Put the ORCA directory first on PATH, or point
qccompute at it with QCCOMPUTE_ORCA_EXECUTABLE or ``executables={"orca": ...}``: on
many Linux desktops ``/usr/bin/orca`` is the GNOME screen reader, not ORCA. Parallel
runs (``pal``) also need the OpenMPI version ORCA was built with, and ORCA stops with
"ORCA has to be called with full pathname" unless it runs by its absolute path, which
qccompute does from the release after 0.15.0 (the one with ``executables=``).

How the codec talks to ORCA (manual: https://www.faccts.de/docs/orca/6.0/manual/):

- ``model.method`` and ``model.basis`` start the simple-input line, ``! method basis``.
  Further simple-input words go in ``model.method`` after the method name, e.g.
  "wB97X-D3 TightSCF" or "b3lyp D3BJ CPCM(water)". Leave ``basis`` out for composite
  methods such as "r2scan-3c".
- The calculation type adds ``! Energy``, ``! EnGrad``, or ``! Freq``.
- ``maxcore`` (MB per process) and ``pal`` (number of processes) become ``%maxcore``
  and ``%pal nprocs ... end``.
- A keyword whose value is a dictionary becomes an input block:
  ``{"scf": {"maxiter": 200}}`` writes ``%scf maxiter 200 end``.
- A keyword set to True adds a simple-input word: ``{"TightSCF": True}`` writes
  ``! tightscf`` (ORCA ignores case), and ``numgrad``/``numfreq`` request
  numerical gradients and Hessians. False or None leaves the word out.
- The molecule is passed in your coordinates and atom order; ORCA does not move it.
- ORCA stops on an unknown simple-input word ("INPUT ERROR ... UNRECOGNIZED OR
  DUPLICATED KEYWORD(S)"); the raised error carries ORCA's output.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy, CalcType.hessian

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="orca",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    # Simple-input words after the method; CPCM(water) is implicit solvent.
    model=Model(method="wB97X-D3 TightSCF CPCM(water)", basis="def2-SVP"),
    # e.g. Model(method="r2SCAN-3c") with no basis, or "uks" for open shells
    keywords={
        "maxcore": 1000,  # memory per process, MB
        # "pal": 4,  # parallel processes (needs OpenMPI)
        #
        # Any ORCA input block, as a dictionary:
        "scf": {"maxiter": 200},
        # "cpcm": {"epsilon": 80.4, "refrac": 1.33},  # a custom solvent, with "CPCM"
        #
        # Numerical derivatives, for methods without analytic ones:
        # "numgrad": True,
        # "numfreq": True,
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=3600,  # seconds before ORCA is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file (orca.gbw, orca.hess, ...)
    # executables={"orca": "/opt/orca/orca"},  # or set QCCOMPUTE_ORCA_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
if results.hessian is not None:
    print("Hessian (Hartree/bohr^2), shape:", results.hessian.shape)
print("ORCA version:", results.provenance.program_version)

"""ORCA transition-state search (OptTS).

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and ORCA on PATH, ahead of
``/usr/bin/orca`` (the GNOME screen reader on many Linux desktops); or set
QCCOMPUTE_ORCA_EXECUTABLE. See single_point.py for installing and running ORCA.

Notes for ORCA transition-state searches (manual:
https://www.faccts.de/docs/orca/6.0/manual/, "Transition State Searches"):

- The codec adds ``! OptTS``. ORCA's eigenvector-following needs a good starting
  Hessian: ``{"geom": {"calc_hess": True}}`` computes the exact one at the first step
  (ORCA otherwise starts from a model Hessian and can miss the saddle point).
  ``recalc_hess`` recomputes it every n steps for difficult cases.
- Start close to the saddle point. This example starts from nearly planar ammonia;
  its inversion transition state is planar, with one imaginary frequency.
- Check the result with a Hessian (single_point.py with CalcType.hessian): a
  transition state has exactly one imaginary (negative) frequency.
- For a scan or NEB to find a starting guess, see ORCA's manual; the codec runs only
  the OptTS step itself.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Nearly planar ammonia, coordinates in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["N", "H", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[
        [0.0, 0.0, 0.25],
        [1.77, 0.0, -0.10],
        [-0.885, 1.533, -0.10],
        [-0.885, -1.533, -0.10],
    ],
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="orca",
    calctype=CalcType.transition_state,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wB97X-D3", basis="def2-SVP"),
    keywords={
        "maxcore": 1000,  # memory per process, MB
        # "pal": 4,  # parallel processes (needs OpenMPI)
        "geom": {
            "calc_hess": True,  # exact Hessian at the first step
            "maxiter": 50,
            # "recalc_hess": 5,  # recompute the exact Hessian every 5 steps
        },
    },
)

output = compute(prog_input)  # timeout=..., collect_files=..., executables=...

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Transition-state energy (Hartree):", results.energies[-1])
print("Transition-state structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)

docs.title: Psi4
docs.text:
Psi4: run through a small driver script and decode the JSON it writes.

The codec writes job.json and a driver script (input.py, from _psi4_driver.py) and runs psi4 input.py -k -o stdout: Psi4 executes the script with its own interpreter, so the caller's Python environment never imports Psi4. The script calls the Psi4 driver for the calculation type and writes results.json; stdout carries Psi4's normal output.

Inputs map to Psi4 as follows:

  • model.method and model.basis form the method string, e.g. "wb97x-d/def2-svp" for psi4.energy("wb97x-d/def2-svp"). Leave basis empty for composite methods or to set basis in keywords.

  • keywords go to psi4.set_options unchanged, so every Psi4 option and its module-scoped form ("scf__maxiter") works as in Psi4's documentation. Two kinds of keyword are not Psi4 options and are routed instead:

  • Driver arguments go to psi4.energy()/gradient()/frequency()/ optimize(): external_potentials (point charges for QM/MM electrostatic embedding, [[charge, [x, y, z]], ...] in bohr), dertype (0 or "energy" for derivatives by finite differences of energies, 1 or "gradient" for Hessians from finite differences of gradients), and project_trans/project_rot (whether frequency analysis removes translations and rotations; Psi4 decides by default).

  • symmetry is the molecule block's point group, e.g. "c1" to turn symmetry off. By default Psi4 detects whatever symmetry the input frame already has.

  • cmdline_args are appended to the psi4 command, e.g. ["-n", "4"] for four threads or ["--memory", "8GB"].

The molecule keeps the input's frame (no_com, no_reorient): Psi4 never moves or rotates it, so gradients, Hessians, normal modes, and trajectories are in the input's coordinates, and symmetry detection only finds symmetry the frame already has. No input field carries atom indices.

Calculation types: energy, gradient, hessian (psi4.frequency: also frequencies, normal modes, and the gradient), optimization and transition_state (psi4.optimize with optking; every step carries its energy and gradient). A transition-state search sets opt_type ts and, unless given, full_hess_every 0 (an exact Hessian at the first step). Every single point also records Mulliken charges in atomic_charges when the method supports them, the gradient on external point charges in point_charge_gradient, and all scalar Psi4 variables in extras["psi4_variables"].

Psi4 1.11 handles point charges correctly only for energies and gradients. Its Hessians with external_potentials either fail or come back wrong (they disagree with finite differences of its own gradients by about as much as the charges change them), and its optimizations reset the molecule to the starting geometry at every step, so they never move. The codec rejects those combinations; for QM/MM geometry optimizations, run geomeTRIC with Psi4 gradients as its child.

"""Psi4 single point: energy, gradient, or Hessian.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and Psi4 on PATH, e.g.
``conda install -c conda-forge psi4`` (add ``pyddx`` for ddX implicit solvent).

How the codec talks to Psi4 (https://psicode.org/psi4manual/master/):

- ``model.method`` and ``model.basis`` become Psi4's method string, e.g. "wb97x-d/def2-svp".
  Leave ``basis`` out for composite methods such as "mp2/cc-pv[dt]z".
- ``keywords`` go to ``psi4.set_options`` unchanged, so use Psi4's option names.
  Module-scoped options are written "module__option", e.g. "scf__maxiter".
- A few keywords are not Psi4 options and are routed where Psi4 expects them:
  ``external_potentials`` (point charges), ``dertype``, ``project_trans``,
  ``project_rot`` (driver arguments) and ``symmetry`` (the molecule block).
- The molecule stays in your coordinates: Psi4 is told not to move or reorient it,
  so gradients and Hessians line up with ``structure``.
- Psi4 errors (unknown option, SCF not converged, ...) raise with Psi4's message.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy, CalcType.hessian

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="psi4",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97x-d", basis="def2-svp"),  # e.g. "b3lyp-d3bj"/"def2-tzvp"
    keywords={
        # Any Psi4 option, exactly as in Psi4's documentation:
        # "scf_type": "pk",  # exact integrals instead of density fitting
        "e_convergence": 1e-8,
        "d_convergence": 1e-8,
        "scf__maxiter": 100,  # module-scoped option
        # "reference": "uhf",  # open shells: also set structure multiplicity
        #
        # Implicit solvent (ddX; needs the pyddx package next to Psi4):
        "ddx": True,
        "ddx_model": "pcm",  # or "cosmo", "lpb"
        "ddx_solvent": "water",
        #
        # Point charges for QM/MM electrostatic embedding, [charge, [x, y, z]] in
        # bohr. Psi4 1.11 handles them only for energies and gradients; the
        # gradient on the charges is returned as point_charge_gradient.
        # "external_potentials": [[-0.8, [0.0, 0.0, 5.0]], [0.4, [1.0, 1.0, 6.0]]],
        #
        # Symmetry: Psi4 detects any symmetry your frame already has without
        # moving atoms. Name a point group to override, or "c1" to turn it off.
        # "symmetry": "c1",
        #
        # Hessians: frequency analysis projects out translations and rotations
        # only at stationary points unless told otherwise.
        # "project_rot": True,
        # "dertype": 1,  # Hessian by finite differences of analytic gradients
    },
    # Arguments for the psi4 command itself: threads and memory.
    cmdline_args=["-n", "1", "--memory", "2GB"],
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=3600,  # seconds before Psi4 is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file in output.results.files
    # executables={"psi4": "/path/to/psi4"},  # or set QCCOMPUTE_PSI4_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
if results.hessian is not None:
    print("Frequencies (cm^-1):", results.freqs_wavenumber)
print("Mulliken charges:", results.atomic_charges)
print("Dipole (e*bohr):", results.scf_dipole_moment)
print("Psi4 variables:", sorted(results.extras["psi4_variables"])[:5], "...")

"""Psi4 geometry optimization with its built-in optimizer, optking.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and Psi4 on PATH, e.g.
``conda install -c conda-forge psi4``.

Notes for Psi4 optimizations:

- optking options are ordinary Psi4 options: ``g_convergence``, ``geom_maxiter``,
  ``step_type``, ``opt_coordinates``, ``full_hess_every``, ... (Psi4 manual, "Geometry
  Optimization").
- Every step in ``results.trajectory`` carries its structure, energy, and gradient;
  the last step also carries the final charges, orbitals, and Psi4 variables.
- The first step is exactly your input structure: Psi4 does not move or reorient it.
- Point charges (``external_potentials``) do not work in Psi4 1.11 optimizations
  (it never leaves the starting geometry), so the codec rejects them. For QM/MM
  optimizations use geomeTRIC with Psi4 gradients; see examples/geometric/.
- For transition states use ``CalcType.transition_state`` (transition_state.py).
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

    program="psi4",
    calctype=CalcType.optimization,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97x-d", basis="def2-svp"),
    keywords={
        # optking settings:
        "g_convergence": "gau",  # or "qchem", "gau_tight", "gau_verytight", ...
        "geom_maxiter": 50,

        #

    },
    cmdline_args=["-n", "1", "--memory", "2GB"],
)

output = compute(prog_input)  # timeout=..., collect_files=..., executables=...

results = output.results

"""Psi4 transition-state search with optking.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and Psi4 on PATH, e.g.
``conda install -c conda-forge psi4``.

Notes for Psi4 transition-state searches:

- The codec sets ``opt_type ts`` and, unless you set it, ``full_hess_every 0``: an
  exact Hessian at the first step, which optking needs to find a saddle point.
  Psi4 has analytic Hessians only for Hartree-Fock, so for DFT it takes finite
  differences of gradients, which it runs by calling ``psi4`` again: keep ``psi4``
  on PATH (not only in ``executables``).
  Setting ``opt_type`` to anything else is an error for this calculation type.
- Start close to the saddle point. This example starts from nearly planar ammonia;
  its inversion transition state is planar, with one imaginary frequency.
- Check the result with a Hessian (single_point.py with CalcType.hessian): a
  transition state has exactly one imaginary (negative) frequency.
- Point charges are not supported here in Psi4 1.11; use geomeTRIC with Psi4
  gradients for QM/MM transition states.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Nearly planar ammonia, coordinates in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["N", "H", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[
        [0.0, 0.0, 0.25],
        [1.77, 0.0, -0.10],
        [-0.885, 1.533, -0.10],
        [-0.885, -1.533, -0.10],
    ],
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="psi4",
    calctype=CalcType.transition_state,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97x-d", basis="def2-svp"),
    keywords={
        "geom_maxiter": 50,
        # "full_hess_every": 3,  # recompute the exact Hessian every 3 steps
        # "step_type": "rs_i_rfo",  # optking's default for transition states
    },
    cmdline_args=["-n", "1", "--memory", "2GB"],
)

output = compute(prog_input)

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Transition-state energy (Hartree):", results.energies[-1])
print("Transition-state structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)

docs.title: TeraChem servers
docs.text:
TeraChem servers through the tcpb client: terachem-fe and terachem-pbs.

terachem-fe talks to a TeraChem frontend server and terachem-pbs to a TeraChem protocol-buffer server (terachem -s <port>), keeping TeraChem and its GPU state running between calculations. Install the client with qccodec[tcpb].

The whole ProgramInput is handed to the tcpb client, which builds the server job itself. model.method must be a method the server protocol knows (hf, b3lyp, wb97x, ...); unrestricted runs set {"restricted": False, "closed_shell": False} rather than a "u" prefix; other keywords follow TeraChem's tc.in names, with values sent as text (write "yes"/"no", not booleans).

The client finds the server through the environment variables TCPB_HOST and TCPB_PORT (terachem-pbs) or TCPB_FRONTEND_HOST and TCPB_FRONTEND_PORT (terachem-fe), read when tcpb is first imported; nothing in ProgramInput sets them.

Calculation types: energy and gradient.

tcpb 0.16.0 builds outputs with the pre-0.19 qcdata models, so this codec refuses to run with it; it needs a tcpb release built against current qcdata.
