examples/terachem-fe/single_point.py

"""TeraChem frontend server single point: energy or gradient.

Requires: ``pip install "qccompute" "qccodec[tcpb]"`` (the tcpb client) and a running
TeraChem frontend; this machine needs no TeraChem install. TeraChem itself runs on a
machine with an NVIDIA CUDA GPU and a TeraChem license. The codec refuses tcpb 0.16.0,
which predates the current qcdata models; it needs a newer tcpb release.

The frontend is a TeraChem protocol-buffer server (``terachem -s 11111``) paired with
an HTTP file server (port 8080 by default) over the server's scratch directory, as in
the Docker images at https://hub.docker.com/r/mtzgroup/terachem. Compared with
``terachem-pbs`` (see examples/terachem-pbs/), the file server lets the client upload
starting orbitals and download TeraChem's output and scratch files.

How the codec talks to the server (tcpb docs: https://mtzgroup.github.io/tcpb-client/):

- The client connects to TCPB_HOST:TCPB_PORT (default 127.0.0.1:11111) and the file
  server at TCPB_FRONTEND_HOST:TCPB_FRONTEND_PORT (default 127.0.0.1:8080). Set these
  environment variables before running, or in the script before ``compute`` as below.
- ``model.method`` must be one of the methods the server protocol knows: "hf",
  "b3lyp", "pbe0", "wb97x", "wb97xd3", "camb3lyp", "blyp", "pbe", "svwn", ...
  Do not prefix "u" for unrestricted; set ``"restricted": False`` (and
  ``"closed_shell": False`` for open shells) in ``keywords`` instead.
- All other ``keywords`` are sent as tc.in options with ``str(value)``, so write
  TeraChem's own values: "yes"/"no", not True/False.
- Starting orbitals: put TeraChem's ``c0`` file (or ``ca0`` and ``cb0``) as bytes in
  ``ProgramInput.files``; the client uploads it and sets the ``guess`` keyword.
- Only energies and gradients are supported.
"""

import os

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy

# Where the TeraChem frontend listens; set before compute() imports the tcpb client.
os.environ.setdefault("TCPB_HOST", "127.0.0.1")
os.environ.setdefault("TCPB_PORT", "11111")
os.environ.setdefault("TCPB_FRONTEND_HOST", "127.0.0.1")
os.environ.setdefault("TCPB_FRONTEND_PORT", "8080")

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="terachem-fe",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97xd3", basis="def2-svp"),  # e.g. "b3lyp"/"6-31gss"
    keywords={
        # tc.in options, as strings TeraChem understands:
        "purify": "no",
        "convthre": "1e-6",  # SCF convergence
        "maxit": "100",  # SCF iterations
        # "pcm": "cosmo",  # implicit solvent
        # "epsilon": "78.39",
        #
        # Open shells (also set structure multiplicity):
        # "restricted": False,  # unrestricted (UHF/UKS)
        # "closed_shell": False,
    },
    # Starting orbitals from an earlier TeraChem run:
    # files={"c0": open("c0", "rb").read()},
)

output = compute(prog_input)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
print("Mulliken charges:", results.extras.get("charges"))
print("Files from the server:", sorted(results.files))

        "maxit": "100",  # SCF iterations
        # "pcm": "cosmo",  # implicit solvent
        # "epsilon": "78.39",
        #
        # Open shells (also set structure multiplicity):
        # "restricted": False,  # unrestricted (UHF/UKS)
        # "closed_shell": False,
        #
        # Extra results from the server:
        # "bond_order": True,  # Meyer bond orders in results.extras
        # "mo_output": True,  # MO coefficients and AO data in results.extras
    },

docs.title: TeraChem
docs.text:
TeraChem: write tc.in, run terachem tc.in, and parse stdout and scratch files.

Inputs map to TeraChem as follows:

  • model.method and model.basis become method and basis; the structure's charge and multiplicity become charge and spinmult. Setting any of these, or run, in keywords is an error.
  • Every other keyword becomes a tc.in line, key value, so TeraChem's own keyword names apply (scf, convthre, dftd, pcm, epsilon, ...). Values are written in lowercase, which suits TeraChem's booleans and options but means case-sensitive values such as file names must be lowercase. TeraChem ignores keywords it does not know, printing only "Unrecognized or unnecessary keywords" in its output, so check the logs when a setting seems to have no effect.
  • cmdline_args are appended to the terachem command.

Calculation types: energy, gradient, hessian (run frequencies; the Hessian and gradient are parsed, frequencies and normal modes are not yet), and optimization, which requires new_minimizer yes in keywords. TeraChem refuses Hessians away from a stationary point unless mincheck false is set. TeraChem keeps the input's coordinates and atom order. No input field carries atom indices.

The orbital files c0 (or ca0/cb0) can seed the next calculation: qccompute's propagate_wfn=True does this between geomeTRIC steps. A run is a failure unless stdout ends with Job finished:.

docs.text:
examples/terachem/single_point.py

"""TeraChem single point: energy, gradient, or Hessian.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and ``terachem`` on PATH.
TeraChem runs only on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs and needs a license file (from PetaChem). A
Docker launcher script that provides ``terachem`` without an install, with the license
given by TERACHEM_LICENSE_PATH, comes with the images at
https://hub.docker.com/r/mtzgroup/terachem.

How the codec talks to TeraChem (manual: https://mtzweb.stanford.edu/terachem/,
or the PDF manual shipped in the TeraChem ``doc`` directory):

- The codec writes ``tc.in``. ``run``, ``coordinates``, ``charge``, ``spinmult``,
  ``method``, and ``basis`` come from ``calctype``, ``structure``, and ``model``;
  setting any of them in ``keywords`` is an error.
- Every other ``keywords`` entry becomes one ``key value`` line in ``tc.in``, so use
  TeraChem's keyword names. Values are written lowercased (``True`` becomes ``true``);
  TeraChem itself expects ``yes``/``no`` for switches. TeraChem ignores unknown or
  misspelled keywords with only an "Unrecognized or unnecessary keywords" warning
  in ``output.logs``, so check there when a setting seems to have no effect.
- Unrestricted methods are spelled in the method name: "uhf", "ub3lyp", ...;
  restricted open shell is "rohf", "rob3lyp".
- Hessians (``run frequencies``) come from finite differences of analytic
  gradients, so they take 6N gradients; the gradient at the input geometry is
  returned as well. TeraChem stops with "Maximum component of gradient is too large"
  unless the structure is a stationary point; ``mincheck false`` turns that check
  off (set below because this example water is not at a minimum; energy and
  gradient runs list it as an unnecessary keyword, which is harmless).
- ``purify no`` is set below because density purification is TeraChem's default for
  large systems and can fail to converge for small molecules.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy, CalcType.hessian

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="terachem",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97xd3", basis="def2-svp"),  # wB97X-D3; e.g. "b3lyp", "ub3lyp"
    keywords={
        # Any tc.in keyword, exactly as in TeraChem's manual:
        "purify": "no",
        "convthre": 1e-6,  # SCF convergence (wavefunction error)
        "threall": 1e-12,  # integral screening threshold
        "maxit": 100,  # SCF iterations
        "mincheck": "false",  # allow Hessians away from a stationary point
        # "precision": "double",  # "single", "mixed" (default), "dynamic", "double"
        # "dftd": "d3",  # empirical dispersion for DFT methods
        # "gpus": "1 0",  # number of GPUs, then the device indices to use
        #
        # Implicit solvent (COSMO); "epsilon" is the dielectric constant:
        "pcm": "cosmo",
        "epsilon": 78.39,  # water
        # "pcm_scale": 1.2,  # scale factor for the cavity atomic radii
        #
        # Excited states (TDDFT/CIS); the gradient is for state "cistarget":
        # "cis": "yes",
        # "cisnumstates": 3,
        # "cistarget": 1,
    },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=3600,  # seconds before TeraChem is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file in output.results.files
    # collect_wfn=True,  # keep the orbitals (scr*/c0) for a later guess
    # executables={"terachem": "/path/to/terachem"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_TERACHEM_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
if results.hessian is not None:
    print("Hessian (Hartree/bohr^2), shape:", results.hessian.shape)
print("Number of orbitals:", results.calcinfo_nmo)
if results.extras.get("excited_states"):
    print("Excited states:", results.extras["excited_states"])
print("TeraChem version:", results.provenance.program_version)

"""TeraChem geometry optimization with its built-in optimizer.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and ``terachem`` on PATH.
TeraChem runs only on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs and needs a license file (from PetaChem).

Notes for TeraChem optimizations (manual: https://mtzweb.stanford.edu/terachem/):

- Only TeraChem's newer optimizer is supported: ``"new_minimizer": "yes"`` is
  required, and the codec raises an error without it.
- Optimizer settings are ordinary tc.in keywords: ``nstep``, ``min_coordinates``,
  ``min_converge_e``, ``min_converge_grms``, ``min_converge_gmax``, ...
- TeraChem does not stop on a misspelled keyword: it prints "Unrecognized or
  unnecessary keywords: These are being ignored." in its output and carries on.
  Check ``output.logs`` for that warning when a setting seems to have no effect.
- Every step in ``results.trajectory`` carries its structure, energy, and gradient,
  read from TeraChem's ``optim.xyz``/``optim_trajectory.xyz`` and its output.
- The first step is your input structure: TeraChem does not move or reorient it.
- Transition-state searches are not supported by this codec; use geomeTRIC with
  TeraChem gradients (``program="geometric"``) instead.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="terachem",
    calctype=CalcType.optimization,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="wb97xd3", basis="def2-svp"),
    keywords={
        "purify": "no",
        "new_minimizer": "yes",  # required
        "nstep": 50,  # maximum optimization steps
        # "min_coordinates": "cartesian",  # default: TRIC internal coordinates
        # Convergence criteria (TeraChem's defaults shown):
        # "min_converge_grms": 3.0e-4,  # RMS gradient (Hartree/bohr)
        # "min_converge_gmax": 4.5e-4,  # largest gradient component
        # "min_converge_e": 1.0e-6,  # energy change (Hartree)
        #
        # Implicit solvent (COSMO):
        # "pcm": "cosmo",
        # "epsilon": 78.39,
    },
)

output = compute(prog_input)  # timeout=..., collect_files=..., executables=...

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Energies (Hartree):", results.energies)
print("Final structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)

docs.title: xtb
docs.text:
xtb: the semiempirical GFN-xTB, GFN-FF, and g-xTB program, run on the command line.

The codec writes structure.xyz and runs::

xtb structure.xyz --<runtype> --chrg <charge> --uhf <unpaired> <method flags> <keywords>

model.method selects the Hamiltonian: gfn0, gfn1, gfn2, gfnff, or gxtb. g-xTB needs the xtb build distributed with g-xTB (https://github.com/grimme-lab/g-xtb); point qccompute at it with executables={"xtb": ...} or QCCOMPUTE_XTB_EXECUTABLE. GFN0 reads its parameter file from the directory named by XTBPATH.

Keywords become command-line flags in xtb's own spelling: {"alpb": "water"} gives --alpb water, {"etemp": 1000} gives --etemp 1000, a list gives several values ({"alpb": ["water", "bar1M"]}), True gives a bare flag, and False or None leaves the flag out. For optimizations, {"opt": "tight"} sets the optimization level. Detailed input ($constrain, $fix, $wall, ...) goes in an xcontrol file supplied through files and named with {"input": "xcontrol"}; such files are passed through verbatim, so atom indices in them are 1-based as xtb expects.

examples/xtb/single_point.py

"""xtb single point: energy, gradient, or Hessian with GFN-xTB, GFN-FF, or g-xTB.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and xtb on PATH, e.g.
``conda install -c conda-forge xtb``. For g-xTB (``method="gxtb"``) use the xtb build
from https://github.com/grimme-lab/g-xtb instead; it also runs every other method.
GFN0-xTB reads its parameter file from the directory named by ``XTBPATH``.

How the codec talks to xtb (https://xtb-docs.readthedocs.io/):

- ``model.method`` picks the Hamiltonian: "gfn0", "gfn1", "gfn2", "gfnff", or "gxtb".
  There is no basis set.
- Charge and multiplicity come from ``structure`` (passed as ``--chrg`` and ``--uhf``).
- ``keywords`` become xtb command-line flags (``xtb --help``): ``{"alpb": "water"}``
  gives ``--alpb water``, ``True`` gives a bare flag, and ``False``/``None`` drop it.
  Flags the codec sets itself (``chrg``, ``uhf``, ``gfn``, ``sp``, ``hess``, ...)
  are rejected.
- xtb only warns about options it does not know and runs without them; the codec
  turns that warning into a failure, so a typo never silently changes the method.
- Detailed settings (``$scc``, ``$wall``, ``$constrain``, ...) go in an xcontrol file
  (``man 7 xcontrol``); see the commented example below. Atom indices in it are
  1-based, as xtb expects.
- g-xTB has no ALPB/GBSA parameters (xtb stops with "No ALPB/GBSA parameters found")
  and xtb 6.7.1 silently ignores ``cpcmx`` with g-xTB, so run g-xTB in the gas phase.
- xtb's Hessian is numerical (finite differences of analytic gradients) and comes
  with harmonic frequencies and normal modes. Do not pass ``cma``: it moves the
  molecule to its principal axes, so results would not match ``structure``.
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

calctype = CalcType.gradient  # or CalcType.energy, CalcType.hessian

# Coordinates are in bohr (Structure.from_xyz / Structure.open read angstrom files).
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,  # open shells: xtb gets multiplicity - 1 unpaired electrons
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="xtb",
    calctype=calctype,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),  # or "gfn1", "gfn0", "gfnff", "gxtb" (g-xTB build)
    keywords={
        # Any xtb command-line flag, without the leading dashes:
        "parallel": 1,  # threads
        "acc": 1.0,  # SCC accuracy; lower is tighter (0.0001 to 1000)
        "iterations": 250,  # maximum SCC iterations
        # "etemp": 300,  # electronic temperature (K); raise it for difficult SCCs
        #
        # Implicit solvent; pick one model (GFN1/GFN2/GFN-FF only, not g-xTB):
        "alpb": "water",  # ALPB; ["water", "bar1M"] also sets the reference state
        # "gbsa": "h2o",  # GBSA (its own solvent names)
        # "cpcmx": "water",  # CPCM-X
        #
        # Extra output, found in the logs or with collect_files=True:
        # "molden": True,  # orbitals in molden.input
        # "wbo": True,  # Wiberg bond orders in wbo
        # "json": True,  # xtbout.json
        #
        # Detailed settings from an xcontrol file (pass it in `files` below):
        # "input": "xcontrol",
    },
    # files={"xcontrol": "$scc\n   temp=500\n$end\n"},
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=600,  # seconds before xtb is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file in output.results.files
    # executables={"xtb": "/path/to/g-xtb/bin/xtb"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_XTB_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Energy (Hartree):", results.energy)
if results.gradient is not None:
    print("Gradient (Hartree/bohr):\n", results.gradient)
if results.hessian is not None:
    print("Frequencies (cm^-1):", results.freqs_wavenumber)
    print("Normal modes (modes, atoms, xyz):", results.normal_modes_cartesian.shape)
print("Partial charges:", results.atomic_charges)
print("xtb version:", results.provenance.program_version)

"""xtb geometry optimization with its built-in optimizer, ANCopt.

Requires: ``pip install qccompute`` (it installs qccodec) and xtb on PATH, e.g.
``conda install -c conda-forge xtb`` (or the g-xTB build of xtb for ``method="gxtb"``,
https://github.com/grimme-lab/g-xtb).

Notes for xtb optimizations (https://xtb-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/optimization.html):

- ``{"opt": "tight"}`` sets the convergence level: "crude", "sloppy", "loose",
  "normal" (default), "tight", "verytight", or "extreme". ``cycles`` caps the steps.
- xtb exits normally when it runs out of cycles; the codec reports that as a failure
  ("failed to converge geometry optimization").
- Each step in ``results.trajectory`` has its structure and energy but no gradient:
  xtb's log records only those.
- Constraints go in an xcontrol file (``$fix``, ``$constrain``, ``$wall``; see
  https://xtb-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/xcontrol.html). Its atom indices are
  1-based, unlike the 0-based indices used elsewhere in qcdata.
- Other keywords become xtb command-line flags, as in single_point.py: solvent,
  accuracy, electronic temperature, threads.
- For transition states, or an optimizer that records gradients at every step, drive
  xtb gradients with geomeTRIC (examples/geometric/).
"""

from qccompute import compute
from qcdata import CalcType, Model, ProgramInput, Structure

# Coordinates are in bohr.
structure = Structure(
    symbols=["O", "H", "H"],
    geometry=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.524, 1.687, 0.48], [1.146, -0.45, -1.354]],
    charge=0,
    multiplicity=1,
)

prog_input = ProgramInput(
    program="xtb",
    calctype=CalcType.optimization,
    structure=structure,
    model=Model(method="gfn2"),  # or "gfn1", "gfnff", "gxtb" (g-xTB build)
    keywords={
        # ANCopt settings:
        "opt": "tight",  # convergence level
        "cycles": 100,  # maximum optimization steps
        #
        "parallel": 1,  # threads
        "alpb": "water",  # implicit solvent; or "gbsa": "h2o"
        # "etemp": 300,  # electronic temperature (K)
        #
        # Constraints from an xcontrol file (pass it in `files` below):
        # "input": "xcontrol",
    },
    # Keep the first O-H bond at its starting length and freeze the oxygen atom.
    # xcontrol atom indices are 1-based: atom 1 is structure.symbols[0].
    # files={
    #     "xcontrol": (
    #         "$constrain\n"
    #         "   force constant=1.0\n"
    #         "   distance: 1, 2, auto\n"
    #         "$fix\n"
    #         "   atoms: 1\n"
    #         "$end\n"
    #     )
    # },
)

output = compute(
    prog_input,
    # timeout=600,  # seconds before xtb is killed
    # collect_files=True,  # keep every output file (xtbopt.xyz, ...) in results.files
    # executables={"xtb": "/path/to/xtb"},  # or QCCOMPUTE_XTB_EXECUTABLE
)

results = output.results
print("Steps:", len(results.trajectory))
print("Energies (Hartree):", results.energies)
print("Final structure (bohr):\n", results.final_structure.geometry)
# Save the trajectory, e.g. to view in a molecule viewer:
# results.save("optimization.json"); results.final_structure.save("final.xyz")
